opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I don't think about "number one" as a title or a ranking. Benchmarks and leaderboards move every few weeks, so if that's your goal, you'll always be anxious and probably chasing the wrong thing.

For me, being at the frontier means working on problems where the answer isn't known yet, and where solving them actually unlocks something for many other people. For a long time my work was in generative models for images and video. Over the years I've become more interested in what I'd call physical AI: models that understand how the world works, how objects move, how actions lead to consequences. That matters if you want robots, autonomous vehicles, or any system that acts in the real world. That's frontier research to me: not just making prettier pixels, but building models that can serve as a foundation for intelligence that interacts with reality.

There's also a responsibility side. If you're in a position to build very large foundation models, you should make them useful to the broader community. A lot of researchers and startups don't have the compute to train these models from scratch. If we can provide strong base models, good tooling, and open them up so people can post-train them for their own robots or applications, the whole field moves faster. I'd rather measure success by how many people build on what we release than by whether we topped one chart.

Finally, it's about the team and the long view. The ideas that matter usually look strange or premature at first. Being at the frontier means having the patience and conviction to keep working on them before everyone agrees they're important, and creating an environment where young researchers feel safe taking those bets.

r001.rationale: The candidate says benchmarks and leaderboards move every few weeks, framing number-one status as short-lived.

r002.rationale: The candidate favors frontier problems that unlock benefits for many people and make models useful to the broader community.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I don't think about it in terms of being number one. If I'm being candid, "number one" is a snapshot. Leaderboards change every few weeks, someone releases a new model, the ranking flips, and then it flips again. If that's what you're chasing, you'll be miserable, because you can never hold onto it.

What matters more to me is whether we're moving the frontier for the problems we actually care about. At NVIDIA, a lot of my work has been around generative models for the physical world: simulation, synthetic data, world models that can understand physics and space and time. In that area, "frontier" means something concrete. Can a robot trained on our synthetic data actually pick things up in a real kitchen? Does an autonomous vehicle see a rare edge case before it encounters it on the road? Those are the benchmarks I care about, and they're not on any public leaderboard.

Being at the frontier also means you're the first one to hit the walls. Nobody has solved the problem ahead of you, so there's no paper to copy. You run experiments for months and most of them fail. So in a sense, being at the front is mostly the experience of being confused more often than everyone else, just a little earlier.

And the last thing I'd say is that frontier research is a team result. The people who get interviewed are a small sample of the people who did the work. When I hear "number one," I think about the engineers who debugged the data pipeline at three in the morning. If it means anything, it means we built a team where that kind of work is possible, and that's the part I'm actually proud of.

r001.rationale: The response calls number one status “a snapshot” and says rankings change every few weeks, so the status is temporary.

r002.rationale: The response describes work on physical-world problems and gives practical examples, but it does not clearly advocate choosing research according to its potential contribution to society.

astra-6.text: To me, being number one means setting the direction, rather than simply getting the highest score on a benchmark. Can you discover something that changes how people build models? Can you give those models capabilities that people couldn’t access before? Benchmarks are useful, but the lead can be temporary. The deeper measure is whether your research creates a lasting advance that other people can build on.

r001.rationale: It says the lead in frontier-model research can be temporary.

r002.rationale: It values research that changes model building and creates lasting advances, but does not say to choose work based on its potential contribution to society.

Are we turning that research into capabilities people can actually use? A ranking is a snapshot. What matters more is whether the team can keep learning, take thoughtful risks, and consistently push the frontier forward.
